identity.title: POCUS 2-point/3-point compression ultrasound of femoral and popliteal veins

technique.how: Linear probe, patient supine with hip externally rotated. Compress the common femoral vein at the saphenofemoral junction (and, for 3-point, the femoral vein in the proximal thigh) and the popliteal vein in transverse view every 1-2 cm; full wall apposition = no thrombus. Non-compressibility or visible echogenic clot = DVT.
technique.prerequisites: Trained operator (formal POCUS DVT training); adequate exposure; ability to compare with contralateral limb if uncertain.
technique.contraindications: None absolute; avoid forceful compression over an obvious large clot; limited by casts, wounds, or severe obesity.

interpretation.positive_finding: Non-compressible common femoral, femoral or popliteal vein is highly specific for proximal DVT (pooled specificity 95-97%; LR+ ~19-30) and justifies anticoagulation pending confirmatory study.
interpretation.negative_finding: A fully compressible 2- or 3-point exam by a trained emergency physician lowers DVT probability substantially (pooled sensitivity 90-96%, LR- ~0.04-0.10) but does not detect isolated calf DVT and misses some isolated femoral-vein clots on 2-point exams.
interpretation.pitfalls: Trainee operators are much less sensitive (77%). Lymph nodes, Baker cysts and superficial veins mimic clot; chronic residual thrombus is non-compressible; 2-point exams miss ~5-8% of isolated femoral vein DVT.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: start anticoagulation and treat as DVT/possible PE source; negative in moderate/high-risk patients: obtain formal duplex or repeat scan in 5-7 days rather than stopping.

estimates.population: Adults with suspected DVT, 16 studies, 2,379 patients; emergency physician-performed compression US
estimates.reference_standard: Colour-flow duplex by radiology/vascular lab or venography
estimates.computed_from: LR+ = 0.961/(1-0.968); LR- = (1-0.961)/0.968 from pooled sens/spec in abstract
estimates.quote: weighted mean sensitivity of EPPU compared to the reference imaging test was 96.1% (95%CI 90.6-98.5%), and with a weighted mean specificity of 96.8% (95%CI:94.6-98.1%)

estimates.population: Adults with suspected DVT, 15 studies 2012-2021, 2,511 examinations; EP-performed 2- or 3-point CUS, all operator levels
estimates.quote: pooled positive and negative likelihood ratio for the same comparisons were, respectively, 19.1 (95%, CI 10.2-35.8) and 0.10 (95%, CI 0.06-0.19)
estimates.location: Results, Primary Outcomes paragraph and Figure 2 (PMC full text); sens/spec also in Abstract

estimates.population: Subgroup: exams performed by EP specialists (attendings) vs trainees
estimates.quote: exams performed by EP specialists (93%, CI 88%-97%) vs trainees (77%, CI 60%-94%). Specificity for EP specialists (97%, CI 94%-99%)

estimates.population: Subgroup: exams performed by EM trainees/residents
estimates.quote: vs trainees (77%, CI 60%-94%). Specificity for EP specialists (97%, CI 94%-99%) was higher than for trainees (87%, CI 76%-99%

estimates.target_condition: Lower-extremity DVT; 3-point vs 2-point protocol, EP specialists only
estimates.population: Subgroup of specialist-performed studies; sensitivity 2-point 0.88 vs 3-point 0.95 (P=0.02)
estimates.quote: Two-point CUS studies performed by specialist EPs had a pooled sensitivity of 88% compared to the 95% found for three-point CUS
estimates.location: Results, Subgroup Analyses and Meta-Regression (PMC full text); value given is 3-point

sources.citation: Pomero F, Dentali F, Borretta V, et al. Accuracy of emergency physician-performed ultrasonography in the diagnosis of deep-vein thrombosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Thromb Haemost. 2013;109(1):137-145.
Hercz D, Mechanic OJ, Varella M, Fajardo F, Levine RL. Ultrasound Performed by Emergency Physicians for Deep Vein Thrombosis: A Systematic Review. West J Emerg Med. 2024;25(2):282-290.
Wells PS, Owen C, Doucette S, Fergusson D, Tran H. Does this patient have deep vein thrombosis? JAMA. 2006;295(2):199-207.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use a negative POCUS to stop workup in high pretest-probability patients, suspected calf or iliac DVT, or when the operator is a trainee without supervision.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Positive POCUS in a patient with dyspnea, hypoxia or hypotension should prompt immediate PE pathway and anticoagulation, not a wait for formal duplex.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Hercz 2024: sensitivity 77% (trainees) vs 93% (specialists); heterogeneity fell markedly when restricted to specialist-performed studies. Pomero 2013 pooled 16 heterogeneous studies with prevalence 7-47%.
safety_scope.skill_assumption: Emergency physician with formal POCUS training (didactics plus supervised scans) performing a 2- or 3-point compression protocol; estimates for specialists do not transfer to untrained users.

extraction_notes: Pomero 2013 figures are from the abstract (pooled bivariate); LRs computed from pooled sens/spec, so their CIs are omitted. Hercz 2024 (PMC OA) provides pooled LRs with CIs directly in Results text; subgroup sens/spec by operator experience and 2- vs 3-point from Abstract/Results. Reference standards were mostly radiology duplex, not venography, so 'misses' relative to radiology duplex, not true DVT, are what these numbers capture.
